<a id="s0-p1"></a>[0¶1] This document is the reference for the `pcrec` command line: the flags of a compile, the listing and query surfaces, the exit codes and the diagnostic conventions. Each flag is stated as `cli/main.c` implements it. `tuning.md` owns the `-f`/`-fno-` optimization-axis family, `limits.md` owns the budget and limit numbers (this document states only which flag sets which), `rxt_format.md` owns the `.rxt` source format, and `docs/pcre2_compliance.md` owns per-construct compliance. The history of this document is `docs/dev/history/cli_record.md`, which is not normative.

<a id="s1"></a>
## 1. Compiling a pattern

```
pcrec [options] -o OUT FILE.rxt...
pcrec [options] -o OUT.c --pattern 'PATTERN'
```

<a id="s1-p1"></a>[1¶1] A positional operand is an input file, never a pattern: each must be an existing `.rxt` source (`rxt_format.md`) and every one given is compiled as §1.1 describes, pooled into one invocation. A literal pattern is given with `--pattern 'X'` (§1.3). The two forms do not combine: a file operand together with `--pattern` is refused. `--` ends option parsing, which is how a file name beginning with `-` is passed; any other argument beginning with `-` that is not a known option is refused as an unknown option. An operand that is not an existing file is refused by name, with a message that points at `--pattern`; it is never reinterpreted as a pattern. A compile needs `-o` and either `--pattern` or at least one file operand; everything else defaults. `--source FILE` and `--fast-or-fail` are not options.

<a id="s1-1"></a>
### 1.1 A file operand: compiling from `.rxt` sources

<a id="s1-1-p1"></a>[1.1¶1] `pcrec -o OUT FILE.rxt...` compiles the `target` declarations of the given `.rxt` sources. It is a compile mode: it honours every compile flag of §1 and writes artifacts. Several files pool their targets into one flat list before the `-o` rule below applies, and a prefix collision across files is refused naming both files.

<a id="s1-1-1"></a>
#### 1.1.1 Which artifacts are built, and where they go

<a id="s1-1-1-p1"></a>[1.1.1¶1] The targets are the file's `target <prefix> = <definition>` lines, in file order, one artifact each. A file that declares no `target` and holds exactly one unnamed pattern block builds the implicit target `rx`. A file with no `target` and anything else builds nothing: it is a library, `pcrec` says so on stderr and exits 0.

<a id="s1-1-1-p2"></a>[1.1.1¶2] A target's definition names a pattern block's `name`, in the file namespace. A name the file does not declare is refused, naming the name and the `lib` chain searched.

<a id="s1-1-1-p3"></a>[1.1.1¶3] `-o` takes one of three forms by the shape of its value, over the pooled target list:

| `-o` value | result | targets |
|---|---|---|
| an existing directory | `<dir>/<prefix>.c` and `<dir>/<prefix>.h`, one pair per target | any number |
| any other name | that `.c` plus its `.h` sibling, as §1.2 | exactly one |
| `-` | one self-contained `.c` on stdout, as §1.2 | exactly one |

<a id="s1-1-1-p4"></a>[1.1.1¶4] `-o FILE` or `-o -` over several targets is refused, naming the targets and the two ways forward (`--target`, or an existing directory). Each target is a separate compile writing its own translation unit.

<a id="s1-1-1-p5"></a>[1.1.1¶5] `--target NAME` builds only the target whose prefix is `NAME`, searched across every file operand given. An unknown name is refused and the message lists the declared targets, each with its file.

<a id="s1-1-2"></a>
#### 1.1.2 Search paths and `--analysis`

<a id="s1-1-2-p1"></a>[1.1.2¶1] `-I DIR` and `--lib-path DIR` are two spellings of one option: a directory added to the search path a `lib "path"` reference resolves against. It is repeatable, the order given is the search order after each source file's own directory, and it is the one option that accumulates rather than replaces. A `lib <store-name>` reference is refused as not in this build. `-I` is also the analysis search path: an analysis `N` is looked up as `DIR/N.rxt` in each `-I` directory in order (`findings.md` §7). So `-I` is legal wherever a bundle is resolved (a file operand, a `--pattern` compile, `--list-analysis`) and is refused with every other query.

<a id="s1-1-2-p2"></a>[1.1.2¶2] `--analysis NAME` (or `--analysis=NAME`) names the analysis a compile reads its subject-aware rates from (`findings.md` §7). It applies to a `--pattern` compile and to each target of a file operand whose configs name none (§1.1.4). Names match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*`; an unknown name refuses the compile, naming the stops searched. It is legal with a compile and with `--list-analysis FILE` and refused elsewhere. An analysis moves speed and never an answer; the artifact records it in `<PREFIX>_FINDINGS`.

<a id="s1-1-3"></a>
#### 1.1.3 Library files

<a id="s1-1-3-p1"></a>[1.1.3¶1] A `lib` file is read, transitively, and its named blocks join the definitions the target's `(?&name)` calls resolve against. The closure is the file's own named blocks first, then each `lib` file's in declaration order, depth first, deduplicated by resolved path (so a cycle terminates). One definition name declared twice in the closure is refused, naming both files. A definition compiles in its own scope: its groups number from 1 in their own space and are re-based into the caller's, its own `flags` seed its parse, and it does not inherit the target's `flags`. What a caller sees of a definition's groups is `match_api.md` §5.5: a library's groups are non-capturing to the caller unless the definition names them, and a named one is delivered by name with a `groups[]` row whose `ref` is the definition's name.

<a id="s1-1-4"></a>
#### 1.1.4 How a target's options compose, and what wins

1. <a id="s1-1-4-p1"></a>[1.1.4¶1] `target … with c1, c2` composes configs by one flat later-wins rule, and `config c from a, b` is that rule one level down.
2. <a id="s1-1-4-p2"></a>[1.1.4¶2] The resulting config composes against the pattern block's own directives by kind: `features` is the union of the two unless the block wrote `features only`; `flags`, `encoding`, `engine` and `budget` are more-specific-wins, that is, the block's.
3. <a id="s1-1-4-p3"></a>[1.1.4¶3] Within one target a config's `pcrec <raw>` flags apply first and the typed directives on top.

<a id="s1-1-4-p4"></a>[1.1.4¶4] The file wins over the command line on the axes the target speaks about, and only those. A command-line flag applies unless the target's configs or block set the same axis, in which case the file's value is used. Every other flag reaches the compile untouched. This inverts the usual convention that an explicit flag beats a file: to have the command line win on an axis the file sets, remove the axis from the file.

<a id="s1-1-4-p5"></a>[1.1.4¶5] `--engine` is the one exception. An explicit `--engine=dfa` or `--engine=vm` on the command line wins over a target's `engine` row, and the conflict is reported on stderr, non-fatally, naming both sources and values:

```
pcrec: FILE:LINE: target 'PREFIX': CLI --engine=dfa and this file's
`engine vm` disagree; using the CLI's explicit choice
```

<a id="s1-1-4-p6"></a>[1.1.4¶6] An explicitly typed `--engine=auto` is indistinguishable from no flag, so it takes the general rule. The exception does not depend on the spelling: a config's raw `pcrec --engine=vm` line is the same axis as the typed row, and within a target the typed row overrides the raw line.

<a id="s1-1-4-p7"></a>[1.1.4¶7] `flags` letters and raw `-f` bits union across sources; they are not file-wins. Bits that contradict each other (`-fprefilter` on one side, `-fno-prefilter` on the other) are refused, never resolved by precedence. Between a config and the pattern block's own `flags`, the block replaces.

<a id="s1-1-4-p8"></a>[1.1.4¶8] `tune` is not an exception: a conflict between an explicit non-default CLI `--tune=` and the file's `tune` row is reported with the file winning:

```
pcrec: FILE:LINE: target 'PREFIX': CLI --tune=min-size and this file's
`tune speed` disagree; using the file's value (--tune is not the
--engine exception)
```

<a id="s1-1-4-p9"></a>[1.1.4¶9] The first words of such a message name the source of the losing value: `CLI`, or "this file's `pcrec` line" when a config's raw `--tune=` supplied it. There is no `--force-tune`.

<a id="s1-1-4-p10"></a>[1.1.4¶10] `--analysis` only fills: a target whose configs name an `analysis` gets that one, and `--analysis` names it only for targets whose configs name none. A disagreement is reported in `tune`'s shape, with the file winning (`… CLI --analysis X and this file's analysis Y disagree; using the file's value (--analysis is fill-only)`). `--analysis` inside a config's `pcrec` line is refused when the file is read; a config names its analysis with its own `analysis` line.

<a id="s1-1-4-p11"></a>[1.1.4¶11] A config's `pcrec <raw>` is re-parsed by this CLI's own option parser, so a flag means the same there as on the command line. It may set compile options only: an output path, `--pattern`, a prefix, a query mode or a file operand is refused. The raw text is split on whitespace with no quoting; no flag takes a value containing a space.

<a id="s1-1-4-p12"></a>[1.1.4¶12] Every artifact stamps `rx_info.name` with the block's `name`, or its `<prefix>` when the block is unnamed (`match_api.md` §6). Diagnostics from a file-operand compile lead with `FILE:LINE` (the owning file), then the target, then pcrec's own pattern offset.

<a id="s1-2"></a>
### 1.2 `-o FILE`: where the C goes

<a id="s1-2-p1"></a>[1.2¶1] `-o FILE` writes `FILE` and a header of the same basename with the extension `.h`: `FILE` ending `.c` has it replaced; otherwise `.h` is appended. The header's basename becomes `pcrec_options.header_name` (`match_api.md` §8.2), which the `.c` file `#include`s.

<a id="s1-2-p2"></a>[1.2¶2] `-o -` is a mode, not a filename: it prints one self-contained `.c` to stdout and writes no header, and the text contains no `#include` of a generated header. It is the form to use to compare two artifacts byte for byte.

<a id="s1-3"></a>
### 1.3 `--pattern 'X'`: the literal pattern

<a id="s1-3-p1"></a>[1.3¶1] The one way to give a pattern text directly; long form only (`-e` is encoding, `-p` is prefix). Exactly one `--pattern` is accepted, and it does not combine with a file operand. Every mode that takes a pattern reads its value, including `--count-groups`, `--emit-ir` and `--emit-facts`.

<a id="s1-4"></a>
### 1.4 `--pattern-esc`

<a id="s1-4-p1"></a>[1.4¶1] Takes the `--pattern` value as double-quoted, escaped text and decodes it before anything else. The vocabulary is the `.rxt` format's subject escapes (`\"` `\\` `\n` `\t` `\r` `\f` `\v` `\xHH`), decoded by the function that decodes a `pattern-esc` block (`rxt_format.md` owns the table).

```
pcrec --pattern-esc -o out.c --pattern '"a\tb\x41"'   # compiles a<TAB>bA
```

- <a id="s1-4-p2"></a>[1.4¶2] The value must be double-quoted, quotes included. An unquoted value, an unescaped `"` inside, a trailing backslash, an unknown escape and `\x` without exactly two hex digits are each refused with what was wrong, exit 1, before anything is compiled or written.
- <a id="s1-4-p3"></a>[1.4¶3] `\x00` is refused, naming K9: the compile entry takes no pattern length, so a NUL-bearing pattern would compile as its prefix. The diagnostic names the lifting trigger, `rx_info.pattern_len`.
- <a id="s1-4-p4"></a>[1.4¶4] It changes only how `--pattern`'s value is read. The value is decoded once, before any mode runs, so every pattern-reading mode reads the decoded text, and a value the decoder refuses is refused in every mode. With no `--pattern` the flag is inert.

<a id="s1-5"></a>
### 1.5 `--version`

<a id="s1-5-p1"></a>[1.5¶1] Prints one line, `pcrec <PCREC_VERSION>` (`lib/pcrec.h`), to stdout and exits 0. The string names the tool and is independent of `abi` (`match_api.md` §6): `abi` versions one artifact's emitted scaffolding, `PCREC_VERSION` changes at a release. The same version is stamped in every artifact's provenance line beside the `abi` digit. It is parsed as `-h`/`--help` is, so inside a config's `pcrec` line it is refused like `-h`.

<a id="s1-6"></a>
### 1.6 `-p PREFIX`: the symbol prefix

<a id="s1-6-p1"></a>[1.6¶1] Every generated identifier is `<PREFIX>_search`, `<PREFIX>_match`, and so on (the entry points are `match_api.md` §3 and §10). `PREFIX` is a C identifier: non-empty, at most `PCREC_MAX_PREFIX_LEN` (60) characters, the first a letter or `_`, the rest alphanumeric or `_`. Anything else is refused with a diagnostic naming the prefix, never truncated or mangled. Default `rx`.

<a id="s1-7"></a>
### 1.7 `-e ENCODING`, `--encoding=ENCODING`

<a id="s1-7-p1"></a>[1.7¶1] Two encodings compile: `byte` (default) and `utf8`. An unknown value is refused with the encoding registry's menu. The encoding is a per-compile scalar (`match_api.md` §9.1), so two patterns in one binary may use different encodings, and `-e byte` and the bare default are byte-identical artifacts.

<a id="s1-7-p2"></a>[1.7¶2] Under `-e utf8` subjects are matched as UTF-8 text: a character is one to four bytes, `.` and a class match a whole character, `\x{…}` accepts code points above `0xFF`, and an ill-formed byte sequence matches nothing unless `-futf-check` (§1.18) is given. A `startpos` passed to `<prefix>_search` must be a character boundary of the encoding; `<prefix>_next_pos` (`match_api.md` §3.1) produces valid positions.

<a id="s1-7-p3"></a>[1.7¶3] `-e utf8` implies modules `unicode-props` and `ucp`: they are enabled for that compile whatever `--features` says, so `\p{…}`, `(*UCP)` and `(*UTF)` need no `--features`. Enabled is not on: UCP semantics still need `(*UCP)` or `--ucp`. The artifact's `PCREC_FEATURE_SET` and `PCREC_FEATURE_MODULES` stamps keep recording the requested set. `(*UTF)` and `(*UTF8)` at pattern start restate the encoding: accepted under `-e utf8`, refused by name under `byte` at every gate state; a pattern may confirm the artifact's encoding and never change it.

<a id="s1-7-p4"></a>[1.7¶4] Under `-e byte`, a code point above `0xFF` written `\x{…}` is a compile error, and a negated class or `.` complements within `[0, 0xFF]`.

<a id="s1-8"></a>
### 1.8 `-i`: case-insensitivity, and which fold

<a id="s1-8-p1"></a>[1.8¶1] `-i` folds case at parse time into the automaton: the emitted matcher carries no flag, branch or `tolower()` for it. Which characters fold is a property of the encoding, because the two relations disagree rather than nest:

| under | a literal or a range folds by | so `(?i)k` matches | and `(?i)\xe9` matches |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--encoding=byte` (default) | the 52 ASCII letters, and nothing else (without `--ucp`) | `k`, `K` | `\xe9` only |
| `--encoding=byte --ucp` | the 52 ASCII letters and the Latin-1 pairs the `--ucp` classes fold | `k`, `K` | `\xe9`, `\xc9` |
| `--encoding=utf8` | Unicode default simple case folding | `k`, `K`, U+212A KELVIN SIGN | U+00E9, U+00C9 |

<a id="s1-8-p2"></a>[1.8¶2] Both are libpcre2's answers at the matching option word (`PCRE2_CASELESS` for `byte`, `PCRE2_UTF|PCRE2_CASELESS` for `utf8`). Consequences:

- <a id="s1-8-p3"></a>[1.8¶3] A caseless class can reach far outside what it wrote: `(?i)[a-z]` under `utf8` matches U+212A and U+017F, because the fold is computed over code points before the byte lowering.
- <a id="s1-8-p4"></a>[1.8¶4] A caseless single character can consume a variable number of bytes (`(?i)k` matching U+212A is a match of length 3); the span reports it.
- <a id="s1-8-p5"></a>[1.8¶5] A named byte set does not gain Unicode partners. `\d`, `\w`, `\s` and the POSIX brackets are ASCII sets, so `(?i)[[:lower:]]` does not match U+212A at either encoding while `(?i)[[:lower:]k]` does. Under `-i`, `\p{Lu}`, `\p{Ll}` and `\p{Lt}` are `\p{L&}` and every other property is unchanged; a property set is never folded on top of that substitution.
- <a id="s1-8-p6"></a>[1.8¶6] A caseless backreference is the one place the fold reaches the artifact, because its operand is subject text: under `utf8` the matcher carries the fold map (table text, outside the emitted-code cap), under `byte` the fold is ASCII-only, and under `--ucp` it is the 56 Latin-1 pairs the `--ucp` classes fold. That table is internal to the artifact and not a caller entry.

<a id="s1-8-p7"></a>[1.8¶7] The fold data is pinned at Unicode 16.0.0 (`third_party/ucd-16.0.0/`), the reference oracle's version; a libpcre2 at another Unicode version disagrees about recently assigned code points.

<a id="s1-9"></a>
### 1.9 `--ucp`: PCRE2_UCP semantics

<a id="s1-9-p1"></a>[1.9¶1] `\d \s \w` and the POSIX classes read Unicode properties: `\d` is `\p{Nd}`, `\s` `\p{Xsp}`, `\w` `\p{Xwd}`, `[:alpha:]` `\p{L}`, and so on (`--list-definitions` prints each under its `DEF_UCP_*` predicate). The pattern spelling is `(*UCP)` at pattern start, combinable with `(*UTF)` in either order; the `.rxt` spelling is `flags u`. It is one bit, `PCREC_UCP` (bit 34), in `pcrec_options.flags`, reflected unmasked in `rx_info.flags`: a semantic axis, not a tuning one (`tuning.md` §4).

- <a id="s1-9-p2"></a>[1.9¶2] It is opt-in: `-e utf8` alone reads `\w` as ASCII. Module `ucp` is implied by `-e utf8` and must be enabled under `byte` (`--features …,ucp`); `--ucp` with the module off is refused by name.
- <a id="s1-9-p3"></a>[1.9¶3] `\h \H \v \V` read PCRE2_UTF's lists under any Unicode encoding, UCP or not (`\h` is U+0009 U+0020 U+00A0 U+1680 U+180E U+2000-U+200A U+202F U+205F U+3000; `\v` is U+000A-U+000D U+0085 U+2028 U+2029), inside a class as at an atom; under `byte` they stay `[\t \xa0]` and `[\n\x0b\f\r\x85]`. `--ucp` and the `(?a…)` letters do not touch them.
- <a id="s1-9-p4"></a>[1.9¶4] `(?aD)`, `(?aS)`, `(?aW)`, `(?aP)`, `(?aT)` each restrict one PCRE2 family to ASCII under UCP (`aW` covers `\w \W \b \B`; `aP` every POSIX class; `aT` `[:digit:] [:xdigit:]`, which `aP` also restricts); `(?a)` sets all five, `(?-a)`/`(?-aX)` unset, and the letters are scoped and survive `(?^)`. Without UCP they change nothing.
- <a id="s1-9-p5"></a>[1.9¶5] Caseless: `[:lower:]` and `[:upper:]` are fold-inert under UCP (`(?i)[[:lower:]]` does not match `A`); an ASCII-restricted set folds by the ASCII fold; everything else by the encoding's fold, except that under `byte` UCP folds the 26 ASCII and 30 Latin-1 letter pairs. A caseless backreference under `byte` follows the same rule: `(\xe9)\1` under `-i --ucp` matches `\xe9\xc9`, and without `--ucp` the compare stays ASCII-only. `\xb5`, `\xdf` and `\xff` have no Latin-1 partner.
- <a id="s1-9-p6"></a>[1.9¶6] Under `byte` the bytes are Latin-1 code points: every UCP set is its Unicode set clamped to `[0, 0xFF]`.
- <a id="s1-9-p7"></a>[1.9¶7] Refused by name: under `-e utf8`, a UCP set wider than `PCREC_UCP_NARROW_MAX_INTERVALS` intervals (`limits.md` §3.8: `\w \W` and the wide POSIX sets), and UCP `\b`/`\B`. Under `-e byte` UCP `\b`/`\B` compile, reading the Latin-1 word set. `(?aW)` and `(?aP)` make a refused construct ASCII again and it compiles. A refusal is never answered with the ASCII meaning.

<a id="s1-10"></a>
### 1.10 `--emit-main`

<a id="s1-10-p1"></a>[1.10¶1] Appends a standalone `main()` taking the subject as `argv[1]`. The emitted program's exit codes are a separate vocabulary from `pcrec`'s own (§3.1): `0` on match, `1` on no-match, `2` on a usage error (wrong argc) and `3` on an honest give-up, with `PCREC_ERR_STEPS`/`_FRAMES`/`_WORK` printed as `steps`/`frames`/`work`. The body and its argv contract are otherwise not part of this document.

<a id="s1-11"></a>
### 1.11 `--no-captures`

<a id="s1-11-p1"></a>[1.11¶1] Emits `RX_NCAPS 1` and forces the DFA engine: the capture-free artifact shape for a group-bearing pattern. Captures are on by default.

<a id="s1-12"></a>
### 1.12 `--trace`

<a id="s1-12-p1"></a>[1.12¶1] Emits an instrumented matcher that prints every resume-frame push and pop and every capture write to stderr as it runs. It is a generation axis: never the default, and the artifact says so.

<a id="s1-13"></a>
### 1.13 `--engine=E`: `dfa`, `vm` or `auto` (default)

<a id="s1-13-p1"></a>[1.13¶1] `dfa` and `vm` are do-or-die: a request the pattern cannot honour is refused, never silently downgraded (for example `--engine=dfa` on a pattern that needs captures is refused, suggesting `--no-captures` or dropping the flag). The refusal is decided from the pattern's AST before any automaton exists. `--engine=vm` also disables the DFA prefilter, so the VM derives the whole span independently of the DFA.

<a id="s1-13-p2"></a>[1.13¶2] `auto` has one exception to do-or-die, and it concerns a cap rather than a construct. A DFA build can overflow a compile-time cap (state count, table entries, the subset-element budget; `limits.md` §3.3, `tuning.md` §2.11) that no AST check sees in advance. Under `auto`, with `-fprefilter` not also requested, that overflow is a selection outcome: the compile falls back to the VM (`RX_ENGINE_WHY` names the cap), or drops an auto-selected prefilter (`tuning.md` §2.5), instead of refusing. `--engine=dfa` and `-fprefilter` keep refusing with "pattern too complex for the DFA engine".

<a id="s1-14"></a>
### 1.14 `--tune=N`: the speed-versus-size dial

<a id="s1-14-p1"></a>[1.14¶1] An ordinal in `-2..+2` (default `0`), or one of the aliases `min-size`, `size`, `balanced`, `speed`, `max-speed`, accepted on equal terms and parsed by `pcrec_tune_parse` (`src/core/tune.c`), so the CLI and the artifact's stamp cannot drift. It sets a group of `tuning.md` §2 axes from one policy table (`tuning.md` §5 owns the table, the reason codes and the acceptance). Every position answers identically over the whole corpus; `<PREFIX>_TUNE`, a closed five-token stamp, is emitted on every artifact, including at `balanced`.

<a id="s1-14-p2"></a>[1.14¶2] A negative value needs the `=` form: `--tune -2` is refused by name (`--tune takes its value with '=' (--tune=-2, --tune=min-size)`), and the aliases, which have no leading dash, are the preferred spelling. An out-of-range value is refused, never clamped (`--tune wants -2..2 or one of min-size, size, balanced, speed, max-speed (got '3')`). A `tune` line in a `.rxt` `config` or `target` block takes the same vocabulary; its precedence is §1.1.4.

<a id="s1-15"></a>
### 1.15 Budgets, capacities and size options

- <a id="s1-15-p1"></a>[1.15¶1] `--step-budget=N` and `--work-budget=N` override the two VM budgets per compile; each takes a positive integer. `--fno-step-budget` is one existence gate for both counters, and there is no `--fno-work-budget`. Defaults, codes and semantics are `limits.md` §2 and §3.1.
- <a id="s1-15-p2"></a>[1.15¶2] `--backtrack-frames=N` raises the resume-stack (and trail) capacity above the compiled-in default, clamped at an internal ceiling when left at auto-sizing; it takes an integer in `1..1,000,000`. The array lives on the C stack, which is what `limits.md` §5 is about.
- <a id="s1-15-p3"></a>[1.15¶3] `--max-nfa-states=N`, `--max-dfa-states-goto=N`, `--max-subset-elems=N`, `--max-auto-dfa-elems=N`, `--max-emit-code-bytes=N` and `--max-emit-bytes=N` raise the matching limit per compile. All six are raise-only: a value below the built-in default is refused (`limits.md` §3.3.2, §8.6).
- <a id="s1-15-p4"></a>[1.15¶4] `--warn-emit-bytes=N` writes one stderr line when an accepted artifact exceeds `N` total emitted bytes. Default `250000`, `0` disables. It is a warning, never a refusal, selects nothing and is stamped nowhere; unlike the caps it may be lowered (`limits.md` §8.7).
- <a id="s1-15-p5"></a>[1.15¶5] `--size-cap=refuse|degrade` chooses what an artifact over either size limit gets. `degrade` (default) walks the size-cap ladder and ships the first smaller form that fits; `refuse` denies every degrading rung so the compile is refused with the ordinary size diagnostic (`limits.md` §8.4). A later `--size-cap=` wins, any other value is refused, and it is one bit for library callers, `PCREC_SIZE_CAP_REFUSE` (bit 41). It is a size policy, not a `-f` axis: an artifact that fits is byte-identical with or without it, and the bit is masked out of `rx_info.flags`. Each rung's own deny flag still applies on its own.

<a id="s1-16"></a>
### 1.16 `--memfn=OPTS`: the search-code kit's options

<a id="s1-16-p1"></a>[1.16¶1] Carries one opaque comma-separated string to pcrec-memory-functions (`memfn/`), the in-tree kit that renders pcrec's search sites. A spelling is `no-NAME` (deny row NAME) or, for a row declared a pair, bare `NAME` (force it); the rows are the `memfn` section of `--list-axes` (`registry.md` §6). pcrec never splits, sorts or looks up an option.

- <a id="s1-16-p2"></a>[1.16¶2] Validation is the kit's (`mf_opts_check`), run once per compile before the parse; its refusal text is shown unchanged after the usual `pcrec: ` lead. An empty string means none. While the kit's registry is empty every non-empty string is refused as an unknown option.
- <a id="s1-16-p3"></a>[1.16¶3] Carriers: the flag; a config's raw `pcrec --memfn=OPTS` line; and `pcrec_options.memfn` (`const char *`, NULL or `""` for none).
- <a id="s1-16-p4"></a>[1.16¶4] Composition (a string value option, `option_sets.md` §2.5a): on the command line the later flag wins; across sources a config's value wins over the command line's, silently.
- <a id="s1-16-p5"></a>[1.16¶5] A row of the kit's `simd` layer is accepted and does nothing at `-fno-memfn-simd` (the default); a scalar-layer row acts at either setting.
- <a id="s1-16-p6"></a>[1.16¶6] The flag sets no bit, moves nothing in `rx_info.flags` and is no `abi` event: with no registered row the artifact is byte-identical with or without it.

<a id="s1-17"></a>
### 1.17 `--features LIST`: the module gate

<a id="s1-17-p1"></a>[1.17¶1] `LIST` is comma-separated module names, a frozen named set (`std1`), `all`, or `none`. An explicit `--features` wins over the bare default, which resolves through `pcrec_default_features` and is `std1`. `std1` is {`classes`, `modifiers`}, and its contents never change after it ships. `--features none` reproduces the bare behaviour of the earliest releases. The flag composes with every mode, not only a compile. An unknown module name is refused by name, listing the vocabulary (`unknown module 'X' (names are --list-syntax's module column; also 'all', 'none', or a named set: std1)`). A construct outside the enabled set is refused with `requires module 'X'`.

<a id="s1-17-p2"></a>[1.17¶2] The library has the same lever: `pcrec_options.features` takes the same vocabulary per `pcrec_compile()` call with no process-global write; NULL there means "no request" rather than `std1` (`match_api.md` §8.2).

<a id="s1-17-p3"></a>[1.17¶3] The modules are the distinct values of `--list-syntax`'s `module` column: `assertions`, `atomic-groups`, `backrefs`, `branch-reset`, `callouts`, `classes`, `comments`, `conditionals`, `extended-classes`, `lookaround`, `misc`, `modifiers`, `named-groups`, `quoting`, `recursion`, `ucp`, `unicode-props`, `vars`, `verbs`. A module's shipped status is read from the `built` column of its rows (`--list-syntax | awk -F'\t' '$4!="" {print $4,$16}' | sort -u`): `built`, `unbuilt`, or a mix for a module that ships a proper subset of its construct (`ucp`, `unicode-props`). For what any one construct does today, with per-construct divergences and caveats, `docs/pcre2_compliance.md` is the authority.

<a id="s1-17-1"></a>
#### 1.17.1 Module `unicode-props`

<a id="s1-17-1-p1"></a>[1.17.1¶1] `\p{…}`/`\P{…}` accepts the Unicode general categories (the one-letter codes, the two-letter ones, `L&`/`Lc`, `Any`) and PCRE2's `Xan Xps Xsp Xuc Xwd`, and the `Script` values the pinned UCD declares except `Katakana_Or_Hiragana` (which no reachable libpcre2 accepts). A script answers to its long name, its four-letter code and any deprecated alias the UCD lists, in three namespaces:

| spelling | denotes |
|---|---|
| `\p{Greek}` | `Script` union `Script_Extensions` |
| `\p{sc=Greek}`, `\p{Script=Greek}` | `Script` alone |
| `\p{scx=Greek}`, `\p{Script_Extensions=Greek}` | the same set as the bare spelling |

<a id="s1-17-1-p2"></a>[1.17.1¶2] The bare spelling is not the `Script` property; that is PCRE2's behaviour (U+0342 has `Script=Inherited` and `Script_Extensions={Greek}`, so `\p{Greek}` matches it and `\p{sc=Greek}` does not). Either separator works (`sc=Greek`, `sc:Greek`), and the prefix and value are case-insensitive and loosely matched. There is no `gc=` namespace, because libpcre2 has none.

<a id="s1-17-1-p3"></a>[1.17.1¶3] Every name works at both encodings, negated as `\P{X}` or `\p{^X}` (the two compose), and inside a class. Under `--encoding=byte` a property is clamped to the Latin-1 universe, so most scripts are the empty set and a pattern whose class is empty compiles to a matcher that never matches. The boolean properties (`\p{Alphabetic}`), `Bidi_Class` (`\p{bc=L}`) and names no libpcre2 has (`\p{Foo}`, block spellings such as `\p{InGreek}`) are refused. The property tables are pinned at Unicode 16.0.0.

<a id="s1-18"></a>
### 1.18 The `-f`/`-fno-` family and the other flags that share its spelling

<a id="s1-18-p1"></a>[1.18¶1] The `-f`/`-fno-` flags, `--unroll=K`, and similar generation axes do not appear in `--help` (they are testing and tuning axes, not user features; `cli/CLAUDE.md` gives the reasoning per flag). Each denies or forces one optimization strategy: most are byte-identity-safe controls for a differential, `-fno-splice-calls`, `-fno-atomic-discharge` and `-fno-ctx-node` can change which engine a pattern gets, and `-fprefilter` is do-or-die like `--engine`. `--work-budget=N` shares the `--flag=value` shape but is a give-up-code axis, which is why it alone is in `--help`. `tuning.md` owns the full list, the force-versus-deny distinction and the byte-identity versus engine-selecting split.

<a id="s1-18-p2"></a>[1.18¶2] `-futf-check` and `-fstartpos-guard=align` share the spelling and are contract axes (`tuning.md` §2.36 and §2.23): they select which answer a call gives. `-futf-check` makes every entry refuse an ill-formed subject with `PCREC_ERR_UTF` (-9), PCRE2_UTF's contract; `-fstartpos-guard=align` moves a mid-character `startpos` forward to the next character start instead of refusing it (`match_api.md` §9.2). Both are off by default and inert under `-e byte`. `-futf-check=extent` is reserved and refused by name (exit 1); `-fstartpos-guard=align` together with `-fno-startpos-guard` is refused as contradictory.

<a id="s1-18-p3"></a>[1.18¶3] `-fcomments` and `-fno-comments` control the emitted artifact's human commentary and nothing else (`tuning.md` §2.24). The default is `-fno-comments`: an artifact carries only its essential comments, the generated-by line naming pcrec and the `abi` and echoing the pattern, and the shared type block's doc-comments. `-fcomments` restores the rest. Deny wins over force. The object file, the comment-excluded source size, every emitted `#define` and the size-cap verdicts are identical under either setting. A `config` block or a file-operand target may set either spelling, and an explicit command-line flag wins (§1.1.4).

<a id="s2"></a>
## 2. Listing and query surfaces

<a id="s2-p1"></a>[2¶1] Ten flags print TSV tables about pcrec itself or about a `.rxt` file; a query takes no pattern and no `-o`, and mixing either in is refused. Seven answer from what this build of pcrec knows: `--list-syntax`, `--list-definitions`, `--list-verbs`, `--list-families`, `--list-axes`, `--list-limits` and `--list-schema`. `--list-source` reads the file named by its value. `--list-analyses` and `--list-analysis` list analyses. The column contract common to all of them (`#` comments, a header row naming every column, append-only columns, resolution by header name) is `table_contract.md`; each table's columns and value sets are `registry.md` (syntax, verbs, families, axes, definitions) or the document named below. This section states what each listing answers. `--flavour NAME` applies to `--list-syntax`, `--list-definitions` and `--explain` only; other listings refuse it, because their rows are not claims about PCRE2 syntax.

<a id="s2-1"></a>
### 2.1 `--list-syntax`

<a id="s2-1-p1"></a>[2.1¶1] Every non-base construct pcrec knows, one row per spelling (columns: `registry.md` §2). `status` and `roadmap` are PCRE2 and base-grammar facts (is this real syntax, is it planned); `built` is orthogonal: whether the owning module's producer has landed, derived live by driving the construct through a gate-forced-open doorway call and never declared by hand (`registry.md` §3). `family` names the canonical spelling a row is grouped under; grouping is index-only and never changes a row's dispatch identity.

<a id="s2-2"></a>
### 2.2 `--list-verbs`

<a id="s2-2-p1"></a>[2.2¶1] The `(*VERB)` names pcrec recognises, in PCRE2's two case-selected tables (`registry.md` §4); `forms` records what libpcre2 accepts, measured.

<a id="s2-3"></a>
### 2.3 `--list-families`

<a id="s2-3-p1"></a>[2.3¶1] One line per family (the rows sharing a `--list-syntax` family key), with `built` combined over every member and `members` listing every spelling, canonical first (`registry.md` §5). It has fewer lines than `--list-syntax`. It takes no `--flavour`.

<a id="s2-4"></a>
### 2.4 `--list-axes`

<a id="s2-4-p1"></a>[2.4¶1] The optimization-axis registry: one row per (axis, candidate) in the emitter's preference order, with the candidate's stamp macro and value, its deny/force bit and CLI spelling, and a description (`registry.md` §6). The stream has two tables: pcrec's axis table, the leading anonymous table, and after it `#section memfn`, the option registry of the search-code kit, one row per option reachable as `--memfn=no-NAME`. A consumer selects the table it reads (`table_contract.md` §4¶6).

<a id="s2-5"></a>
### 2.5 `--list-definitions`

<a id="s2-5-p1"></a>[2.5¶1] The replacement/definition table: one row per (row, definition-array entry), joining `--list-syntax` on `kind`, `selector` and `syntax`, with `order`, `predicate` (the option-scope tag's name, a closed vocabulary), `definition` and `applies` (`registry.md` §9). It reports what the table says a construct's substitution is, not evidence that the substitution parses or matches the same strings.

<a id="s2-6"></a>
### 2.6 `--list-limits`

<a id="s2-6-p1"></a>[2.6¶1] Every numeric limit in `src/core/limits.def`, one row per limit: `name`, `value`, `unit`, `kind` (`compile budget`, `runtime capacity`, `size cap`, `selection knee`, `identifier cap`), `override` (`flag`, `-D`, `flag+-D`, `none`), `anchor` (the `limits.md` section documenting the number, empty when none does) and `desc`. A row's value is spliced into the generating site, so the dump and the compiled binary cannot disagree about a limit's value. `pcrec_limits_tsv` renders the same table (`limits.md` §3.4a).

<a id="s2-7"></a>
### 2.7 `--list-schema`

<a id="s2-7-p1"></a>[2.7¶1] The `.rxt` format's own schema: one row per (scope, line-kind), in two named sections, `schema` and `surface` (the declared non-coverage: what the schema does not claim to validate, and why). `rxt_format.md` ("The schema and its surface") is the column contract. The dump walks the same table the parser enforces. Trailer comments `# schema-rows: N`, `# wave-built: N` and `# wave-reserved: N` give a consumer the table's row total and the wave boundaries.

<a id="s2-8"></a>
### 2.8 `--list-source FILE`

<a id="s2-8-p1"></a>[2.8¶1] The `.rxt` source file named by the option's value, as written: one row per head declaration and per pattern block in file order, followed by the `#section` blocks `provenance`, `variants`, `cases` and `aux` when non-empty. The column table, the `kind` vocabulary, the escaping rule and the "as written, never resolved" contract are `rxt_format.md`. The file is the option's value because the positional slot is a file operand's (§1), and a positional operand in any query mode is refused. A file that parses but declares no pattern block prints its head rows and exits 0; a file whose head does not parse exits 1 with a diagnostic naming the file, the line and the construct. A resolved view (`--list-source --resolved`) is not built.

<a id="s2-9"></a>
### 2.9 `--list-analyses`, `--list-analysis NAME|FILE`

<a id="s2-9-p1"></a>[2.9¶1] `--list-analyses` has one row per analysis built into the library (`-I` directories are never enumerated) and takes no `-I`. `--list-analysis NAME` prints the chain this invocation resolves (honouring `-I`), what each (query, encoding) answers from with the digest a stamp would carry, and the named bundle's rows, declarations and provenance. `--list-analysis FILE` (any value that is not an analysis name) prints the per-target view of a `.rxt` file. Sections and columns: `findings.md` §8.

<a id="s2-10"></a>
### 2.10 `--emit-ir`: the VM program listing

<a id="s2-10-p1"></a>[2.10¶1] A query that takes a pattern, takes no `-o` and emits no C. It prints the VM program listing (labels, instructions with branch targets, choice points with preference order, capture-slot assignments, island boundaries, callout sites and the artifact-wide summary facts) and exits. It is VM-only: on a pattern that compiles to the DFA engine it refuses, naming `--engine=vm`. The output is `table_contract.md` TSV with every table a named `#section`; `ir_listing.md` §3 specifies the sections. A consumer resolves columns by name and treats the listing as a debug surface: complete for control structure, lossy on operands. Every row derives from the event stream the emitting call appended, so the listing cannot drift from the emitter. `--emit-dot` does not exist.

<a id="s2-11"></a>
### 2.11 `--emit-facts[=ENC,...]`: the pattern-facts listing

<a id="s2-11-p1"></a>[2.11¶1] A query like `--emit-ir`: it takes a pattern, takes no `-o` and emits no C. It runs the ordinary compile to completion and prints every fact pcrec concluded about the pattern, its status, whether a pass asked for it and why, followed by the artifact's decision stamps. Every compile option applies unchanged. The bare flag lists the compile under the `-e` in effect; `=ENC,...` runs one compile per listed encoding and concatenates the rows, each naming its encoding, and an unknown encoding name is refused as `-e` refuses it. It works on every engine, composes with no other query mode, refuses `--flavour`, and a pattern pcrec refuses is refused with the compile's own diagnostic. The output is `table_contract.md` TSV in two sections, `facts` and `decisions`, specified by `facts_listing.md` §4. It is a debug listing: no `abi` number, and it never refuses a compile that succeeded.

<a id="s2-12"></a>
### 2.12 `--explain SYNTAX`

<a id="s2-12-p1"></a>[2.12¶1] A cross-source query: it prints the registry row's declared attribution beside what the live doorway parser answers for that text and compares them. Agreement is the expected case; a disagreement is a pcrec defect, surfaced as exit 3 (§3.1). `--flavour` restricts it; only `pcre2` exists.

<a id="s2-13"></a>
### 2.13 `--count-groups --pattern PATTERN`

<a id="s2-13-p1"></a>[2.13¶1] Runs the real parser, parse only, nothing emitted, and prints the capturing-group count (`--count-groups --pattern 'a(b)(c(d))'` prints `3`). A pattern pcrec refuses is refused with the diagnostic a compile would give.

<a id="s2-14"></a>
### 2.14 `--probe-ask WANT CONSTRUCT`

<a id="s2-14-p1"></a>[2.14¶1] An internal, test-only query, not part of the public surface. It drives one construct doorway once at ask level `claim`, `verdict` or `result` and reports the parser cursor before and after. `CONSTRUCT` is the flag's own second argument, a syntax fragment consumed as `--explain`'s argument is. Its home is `tests/spec_mod0/CLAUDE.md` and `docs/testing.md`.

<a id="s3"></a>
## 3. Diagnostics

<a id="s3-1"></a>
### 3.1 Exit codes

| exit | when |
|---|---|
| `0` | success: a compile that wrote its files, or a query that answered |
| `1` | a usage error, a compile refusal, or a query that could not be answered (an unclosed group, an unknown option, an unwritable output path) |
| `3` | `--explain` dissent only: the registry's declared attribution disagrees with what the live doorway parser answers |

<a id="s3-1-p1"></a>[3.1¶1] These are `pcrec`'s own exit codes. They are a separate vocabulary from an `--emit-main` binary's exit codes (§1.10) and from a give-up code (`PCREC_ERR_STEPS` and the others, a C-level return value of a generated function, `match_api.md` §4): three numbering schemes that share small integers and nothing else.

<a id="s3-2"></a>
### 3.2 The diagnostic class tag

<a id="s3-2-p1"></a>[3.2¶1] Every diagnostic pcrec emits while reading a `.rxt` source file (a file operand, `--list-source`) carries a machine-read class tag naming which rule was violated, ahead of the message:

```
pcrec: [structure-attachment] path/to/file.rxt:12: indented line continues nothing (...)
```

<a id="s3-2-p2"></a>[3.2¶2] The tag's position is stable (first, in square brackets, before the `file:line:`) and its set is closed:

| class | what was violated |
|---|---|
| `structure-attachment` | where a line attaches, or may not |
| `unknown-token-in-scope` | the kind has no schema row in this scope, or has one whose wave is above this build's |
| `schema-constraint` | a declared rule over lines: cardinality, a closed set, a uniqueness or resolution rule |
| `value-shape` | the line attached and is legal here; its value does not parse |

<a id="s3-2-p3"></a>[3.2¶3] The sentence beside the tag is not a contract. The tag exists so a consumer can compare which rule fired rather than an exit code. It is delivered on stderr only; there is no structured output mode.

<a id="s3-3"></a>
### 3.3 The compatibility tiers, caller-side

- <a id="s3-3-p1"></a>[3.3¶1] What a pattern matches, for syntax pcrec implements, is exact; a wrong match is always a bug.
- <a id="s3-3-p2"></a>[3.3¶2] Whether a construct is real PCRE2 syntax, and which module owns it, is exact; naming a module that will never implement a construct, or rejecting syntax PCRE2 accepts, is a defect.
- <a id="s3-3-p3"></a>[3.3¶3] The wording, error number and PCRE2's own offset for something pcrec does not implement are not promised. `requires module 'X'` discharges the obligation in full: match on the module name, never on the sentence around it.
- <a id="s3-3-p4"></a>[3.3¶4] pcrec's own offset is exact. A diagnostic's offset points at a real position in the pattern that pcrec's own parse reached, checked against pcrec's convention and not against the number PCRE2 would report for the same input (`[[.a[.b.].]` reports the nested opener, offset 4, where PCRE2 reports offset 9).

<a id="s3-4"></a>
### 3.4 `requires module 'X'`

<a id="s3-4-p1"></a>[3.4¶1] The permanent form of a refusal for a construct pcrec recognises but has no producer for. It carries no promise of a timeline; the `built` column of `--list-syntax` is the status.

<a id="s4"></a>
## 4. What the CLI does not do

- <a id="s4-p1"></a>[4¶1] There is no runtime: `pcrec` is an ahead-of-time compiler, and no mode matches a pattern against a subject without generating and compiling C. `--emit-main`'s appended `main()` (§1.10) is the closest, and it still goes through a real `cc`.
- <a id="s4-p2"></a>[4¶2] There are no multi-pattern compilation units. A file operand (§1.1) compiles several patterns in one invocation, but each target is its own compile writing its own translation unit: one artifact per unit. A single unit holding several named, cross-referencing patterns is not built.
- <a id="s4-p3"></a>[4¶3] There is no `--lib FILE`, and `--lib-path` is not it: it supplies the search path for `lib "path"` references, and the files it finds are read (§1.1.3).
- <a id="s4-p4"></a>[4¶4] There is no `--emit-dot` and no DFA listing; `--emit-ir` (§2.10) is VM-only.
